A finite disjoint family of essential smooth circles can be carried by a jointly smooth ambient isotopy of $T$ to parallel affine circles. Likewise two smooth spanning arcs of a parametrized annulus with the same endpoints and relative winding number are smoothly ambient isotopic relative to any collars on which they already agree. When disjoint, they have a smooth disk-strip parameter; disjoint essential circles in a parametrized annulus have smooth annulus-strip parameters. All isotopies may be stationary near their time endpoints.

For real $\theta$, define the Lobachevsky function
$$
\Lambda(\theta)=-\int_0^\theta \log|2\sin u|\,du,
$$
where the integral is interpreted improperly at zeros of $\sin u$.

derivations.claim: For $|w|<1$, integrating the uniformly convergent geometric series on compact subdisks gives $-\log(1-w)=\sum_{n\ge1}w^n/n$. Taking real parts at $w=re^{2iu}$, where $0<r<1$, yields $-\log|1-re^{2iu}|=\sum_{n\ge1}r^n\cos(2nu)/n$. This series is uniformly absolutely convergent in $u$ for fixed $r$, so integrating from $0$ to $\theta$ gives $-\int_0^\theta\log|1-re^{2iu}|\,du=\frac12\sum_{n\ge1}r^n\sin(2n\theta)/n^2$.

For $r\ge1/2$, $|1-re^{2iu}|^2=(1-r)^2+4r\sin^2u$, so $\sqrt2|\sin u|\le |1-re^{2iu}|\le2$. Therefore $|\log|1-re^{2iu}||$ is bounded by a constant plus $|\log|\sin u||$, which is integrable on bounded intervals. Dominated convergence sends the integral in step 1.1 to $\Lambda(\theta)$ as $r\uparrow1$; the series converges uniformly in $\theta$ because $\sum n^{-2}<\infty$. This proves the Fourier expansion on $[0,\pi]$ and continuity there.

The defining integrand is even, so $\Lambda$ is odd. Its derivative away from the integral's singularities is $-\log|2\sin\theta|$, a $\pi$-periodic function; the Fourier formula gives $\Lambda(0)=\Lambda(\pi)=0$, so the integral of this derivative over each period is zero. Hence $\Lambda(\theta+\pi)=\Lambda(\theta)$ for every real $\theta$. Substitution $\theta=\pi/2$ in the Fourier series gives $\Lambda(\pi/2)=0$.

The identity $|2\sin(2u)|=|2\sin u|\,|2\sin(u+\pi/2)|$ and substitution $v=2u$ in the defining integral give $\Lambda(2\theta)=2\Lambda(\theta)+2\Lambda(\theta+\pi/2)-2\Lambda(\pi/2)$. Step 3.1 gives the stated duplication identity.

In the Fourier series at $\theta=\pi/3$, $\sin(2n\pi/3)$ cycles through $\sqrt3/2,-\sqrt3/2,0$, so grouping successive triples gives the stated positive series. For $a=3k+1$, $a^{-2}-(a+1)^{-2}=(2a+1)/(a^2(a+1)^2)\le2/a^3\le2/(27k^3)$ for $k\ge1$. For $N\ge1$, the tail after $k=0,\ldots,N$ is at most $\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\frac2{27}\sum_{k>N}k^{-3}\le\frac{\sqrt3}{4}\frac2{27}\int_N^\infty x^{-3}\,dx=\frac{\sqrt3}{108N^2}\le\frac{\sqrt3}{72N^2}$.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth $3$-manifold. A properly embedded surface is **two-sided** if it has a product neighbourhood $F\times[-1,1]$ in $M$. A **compressing disk** for a two-sided surface $F$ is an embedded disk $D\subset M$ with $\operatorname{int}(D)\cap F=\varnothing$ and $\partial D$ an essential simple closed curve in $F$; $F$ is **incompressible** if it has no compressing disk. A **boundary-compressing disk** is an embedded disk $D$ with $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$, where $\alpha=D\cap F$ is an arc not cutting off a disk in $F$, $\beta=D\cap\partial M$, and $\operatorname{int}(D)$ misses $F\cup\partial M$; $F$ is **boundary-incompressible** if it has no such disk. A surface is **boundary-parallel** if it cobounds a product with a subsurface of $\partial M$, and it is **essential** if it is incompressible, boundary-incompressible, and not boundary-parallel. $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. An incompressible torus is boundary-parallel if it cobounds a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with a component of $\partial M$; $M$ is **atoroidal** if every incompressible torus is boundary-parallel. A **Seifert fibration** is a decomposition into circles with local models given by fibered solid tori; in the model $(D^2\times S^1)/\langle(z,w)\mapsto(e^{2\pi i/q}z,e^{2\pi ip/q}w)\rangle$, where $\gcd(p,q)=1$, the core fiber has multiplicity $q$. Fibers of multiplicity $1$ are **regular** and those of multiplicity greater than $1$ are **exceptional**. A finite family of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori is a **JSJ system** if every component obtained by cutting $M$ along the family is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. It is **inclusion-minimal** if no proper subfamily is a JSJ system. Atoroidal does not mean hyperbolic.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Assume AC. Let $M$ and $N$ be nonempty connected oriented complete finite-volume Riemannian three-manifolds of constant curvature $-1$. There is no knot, compactness, or cusp-number restriction. Every isomorphism $\theta:\pi_1(M)\to\pi_1(N)$, up to conjugacy from basepoint changes, is induced by a unique isometry $I:M\to N$. The isometry is properly homotopic to every proper homotopy equivalence inducing that outer isomorphism. Its orientation agrees with that of such an equivalence, and the two Riemannian volumes are equal.

Use the upper half-space model
$$\mathbb H^3=\{(x+iy,t):x,y\in\mathbb R,\ t>0\},\qquad ds^2=t^{-2}(dx^2+dy^2+dt^2),$$
whose ideal boundary is $\mathbb C\cup\{\infty\}$. An oriented ideal tetrahedron in normalized position has ideal vertices $0,1,\infty,z$, where $\operatorname{Im}z>0$. Its three edge-shape parameters are
$$z,\qquad z'=\frac1{1-z},\qquad z''=\frac{z-1}{z},$$
Assign $z$ to the edges $0\infty$ and $1z$, $z'$ to $1\infty$ and $0z$, and $z''$ to $z\infty$ and $01$. The parameter at a corner of a truncated ideal vertex triangle is the parameter of the incident edge. In a triangulated oriented torus link of ideal vertices, use oriented normal paths: paths avoiding link vertices, transverse to link edges, and meeting each triangle in arcs joining distinct sides, each cutting off one corner. Represent a loop by such a path before computing its cusp multiplier. For a chosen normal path $\gamma$, its cusp multiplier $H(\gamma)$ is the product of the corner parameters it cuts off, using the parameter when the corner is on its left and its reciprocal when the corner is on its right.

For an oriented ideal tetrahedron with normalized vertices $0,1,\infty,z$ and $\operatorname{Im}z>0$, its three edge-shape parameters are $z$, $z'=1/(1-z)$, and $z''=(z-1)/z$. They satisfy $zz'z''=-1$, and their arguments in $(0,\pi)$ are the three dihedral angles, whose sum is $\pi$. For $\omega=e^{i\pi/3}$, the choice $z=\omega$ gives $z=z'=z''=\omega$ and all six dihedral angles equal to $\pi/3$.

Let an orientable finite ideal triangulation have exactly one ideal vertex, whose link is a torus. Suppose its tetrahedra carry positive shapes whose edge products equal $1$ and whose dihedral angles sum to $2\pi$ around every edge. If the cusp multipliers $H(\alpha)$ and $H(\beta)$ are $1$ for a basis $\alpha,\beta$ of the torus fundamental group, then the glued hyperbolic metric is complete at that cusp.

Let $\Gamma\subset\mathbb C$ be a rank-two lattice acting on $\mathbb H^3$ by horizontal translations, and let
$$
C=\{(x+iy,t):t\ge1\}/\Gamma
$$
be the quotient of the horoball $t\ge1$. If $A$ is the Euclidean area of a fundamental parallelogram for $\Gamma$, then the end is at infinite hyperbolic distance and $\operatorname{Vol}(C)=A/2$.

Every regular ideal tetrahedron in hyperbolic three-space has volume
$$v_3=3\Lambda(\pi/3) =\frac{3\sqrt3}{4}\sum_{k=0}^{\infty} \left(\frac1{(3k+1)^2}-\frac1{(3k+2)^2}\right).$$

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle
$$
D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.
$$
Choose $\epsilon$ so that $D_\epsilon\nu(K)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The fibre norm, tubular map, and radius are part of the chosen tubular data. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Assume countable choice. For a smooth oriented knot with a chosen product tubular neighbourhood $N(K)\cong S^1\times D^2$, let $\mu$ be the positive fibre meridian and let $\sigma$ be the product section $s\mapsto(s,1)$ of $T_K=\partial N(K)\cong S^1\times S^1$. Then $T_K=\partial E_K$ is a torus and $[\mu],[\sigma]$ form a basis of $H_1(T_K;\mathbb Z)$. The curve $\sigma$ is a product section; this statement does not assert that it is the preferred zero-homology longitude.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $Q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ be the base configuration of
[[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]], with $h=\frac{1}{4(n+1)}$ and
$q_j=((2j-n-1)h,0)$. Fix an index $i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$. The two adjacent
base points are

$$q_i=\bigl((2i-n-1)h,0\bigr),\qquad q_{i+1}=\bigl((2i+1-n)h,0\bigr),$$

their **midpoint** is $m_i:=(q_i+q_{i+1})/2=((2i-n)h,0)=q_i+(h,0)$, and their
**support disc** is the open disc

$$U_i:=\bigl\{w\in\mathbb R^2:\lVert w-m_i\rVert_2<\tfrac32h\bigr\}.$$

The support disc contains the two base points $q_i,q_{i+1}$, whose distance from
$m_i$ is $h$, and it contains no other base point: for $k<i$ one has
$\lVert q_k-m_i\rVert_2=(2(i-k)+1)h\ge 3h$ and for $k>i+1$ one has
$\lVert q_k-m_i\rVert_2=(2(k-i)-1)h\ge3h$, both exceeding $\tfrac32h$. Moreover
$U_i\subseteq D^\circ$, because every point of $U_i$ has norm at most
$\lVert m_i\rVert_2+\tfrac32h\le(n-2)h+\tfrac32h<(n+1)h<1$. Finally
$U_i\cap U_j=\varnothing$ whenever $|i-j|>1$, since then the midpoints are at
distance $2|i-j|h\ge4h>3h$, twice the radius.

**The positive half twist.** Define $\rho\colon I\to\mathbb R^2$, the
**anticlockwise diamond path**, by

$$\rho(t):=\begin{cases}\bigl(2th-h,\,-2th\bigr),&0\le t\le \tfrac12,\\[2pt] \bigl(2th-h,\,2th-2h\bigr),&\tfrac12\le t\le1.\end{cases}$$

Thus $\rho(0)=(-h,0)$, $\rho(\tfrac12)=(0,-h)$, $\rho(1)=(h,0)$, and $\rho$ is
continuous, piecewise linear, and satisfies $\lVert\rho(t)\rVert_2\le h$ for all
$t$ with $\rho(t)\neq0$ throughout. The **elementary half twist at $i$**, written
$\sigma_i$, is the tuple of motions

$$(\sigma_i)_i(t):=m_i+\rho(t),\qquad (\sigma_i)_{i+1}(t):=m_i-\rho(t),\qquad (\sigma_i)_k(t):=q_k\ \ (k\notin\{i,i+1\}).$$

It is a braid based at $Q$
([[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]],
[[def-continuous-map-top]]): the two moving points stay in $U_i$ and are
antipodal about $m_i$, so they are distinct; every other point is fixed and lies
outside $U_i$; and the endpoint permutation is the transposition of $i$ and
$i+1$, since $(\sigma_i)_i(1)=m_i+(h,0)=q_{i+1}$ and
$(\sigma_i)_{i+1}(1)=m_i-(h,0)=q_i$.

The words *positive* and *anticlockwise* refer to the fixed orientation of the
plane of the disc and to the fixed planar projection whose horizontal axis
contains $Q$: the moving pair turns through the half turn anticlockwise, the
label $i$ passing below its midpoint and the label $i+1$ above. Together with
the first-under-second stacking convention of
[[prop-stacking-of-geometric-braids-is-well-defined]] this fixes the sign
convention for every signed crossing on this page and its companion.

**The opposite half twist.** The **opposite** (clockwise) half twist at $i$ is
defined by the reflected path

$$\rho^{-}(t):=\bigl(\rho_1(t),-\rho_2(t)\bigr),$$

through the motions $(\sigma_i^{-})_i(t):=m_i+\rho^{-}(t)$,
$(\sigma_i^{-})_{i+1}(t):=m_i-\rho^{-}(t)$ and
$(\sigma_i^{-})_k(t):=q_k$ for $k\notin\{i,i+1\}$. It is again a braid supported
in $U_i$ with endpoint permutation the transposition of $i$ and $i+1$; its pair
turns through the same half turn clockwise, the label $i$ passing above the
midpoint. The two motions are not equal, and they are not related by a
reparametrisation of the height: they are the two signed crossings of the pair.

**The opposite motion is the group inverse.** For a braid $\beta$ the reversed
braid $\overline\beta_j(t)=z_{\pi(\beta)^{-1}(j)}(1-t)$ represents
$[\beta]^{-1}$ in the group $G_n$
([[thm-geometric-braids-form-a-group]]). For $\beta=\sigma_i$ one computes
$\overline{\sigma_i}=\sigma_i^{-}$: reversing the height and relabelling by the
transposition of $i$ and $i+1$ sends $\rho(t)=m_i+(\rho_1,\rho_2)$ to the
motion with relative path $-\rho(1-t)$, which is the reflected path
$\rho^-$ traversed from $t=0$ to $t=1$. Hence

$$[\sigma_i^{-}]=[\sigma_i]^{-1}\qquad\text{in }G_n .$$

**Elementary cases.** For $n\le1$ there is no index $i$ with $1\le i\le n-1$,
and there are no elementary half twists; the assertions above are vacuous. For
$n\ge2$ and $1\le i\le n-1$ both $[\sigma_i]$ and $[\sigma_i^{-}]$ are
nonidentity elements of $G_n$, since their endpoint permutations are
transpositions, which are not the identity permutation.

**Two letters do not commute in general.** For adjacent indices the supports
$U_i$ and $U_{i+1}$ overlap and no commutation is asserted;
[[lem-geometric-far-commutativity]] proves commutativity only for disjoint
supports.

Let $n\in\mathbb N$ and let $Q=(q_1,\dots,q_n)$ be the base configuration of
[[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]]. Write

$$G_n:=\{[\beta]:\beta\ \text{a braid based at}\ Q\}$$

for the set of braid isotopy classes relative to the top and bottom
([[def-braid-isotopy-relative-top-and-bottom]]), and let $[\gamma][\beta]:
=[\gamma\star\beta]$ be the stacking of
[[prop-stacking-of-geometric-braids-is-well-defined]]. Then:

**(a)** $G_n$ is a group ([[def-group]]) with this operation. Its identity is
the class $[e]$ of the trivial braid $e_j(t):=q_j$, and the inverse of
$[\beta]$, for $\beta=(z_1,\dots,z_n)$ with endpoint permutation $\pi(\beta)$,
is the class of the **reversed braid**

$$\overline\beta_j(t):=z_{\pi(\beta)^{-1}(j)}(1-t)\qquad(t\in I,\ 1\le j\le n).$$

**(b)** The endpoint permutation map

$$\pi\colon G_n\longrightarrow S_n,\qquad[\beta]\longmapsto\pi(\beta),$$

is a well-defined group homomorphism
([[def-finite-symmetric-group-and-permutation-notation]]).

The construction is choice-free: all motions and reparametrisations used are
given by explicit formulas.

Let $n\ge0$ and let $\beta=(z_1,\ldots,z_n)$ be a geometric braid with
the fixed real basepoints $q_j=((2j-n-1)/(4(n+1)),0)$ and endpoint
permutation $\pi$, as in [[def-geometric-braid-with-setwise-endpoints]].
Identify the disk with $\{x\in\mathbb C:|x|<1\}$ and put
$$V=(D^\circ\times[0,1])/((x,1)\sim(x,0)).$$
The quotient and its topology use [[def-product-topology]] and the circle
$\mathbb R/\mathbb Z$ of [[def-circle-as-real-line-mod-integers]].
The interval images
$$s_j=\{[(z_j(t),t)]:0\le t\le1\},\qquad \operatorname{cl}(\beta)=\bigcup_{j=1}^n s_j$$
are the **closure in the open solid torus**. In general an individual
$s_j$ is an interval image, not a closed circle: its last point is the
first point of $s_{\pi(j)}$.

**Components and orientation.** For a cycle
$(j,\pi(j),\ldots,\pi^{k-1}(j))$ concatenate these $k$ strand maps in
that order, with parameter in $[0,k]$. Their endpoints agree in $V$,
so the concatenation factors through $\mathbb R/k\mathbb Z$.
It is injective on this circle: points at distinct nonintegral heights
can agree only when their parameters have the same fractional part,
and the distinct strands at that height have distinct disk coordinates;
at integral heights only the specified adjacent endpoints agree.
Thus each cycle gives an embedded circle. Different cycles give
disjoint circles, and every strand belongs to exactly one cycle.
These circles are precisely the connected components of the closure.
The orientation is increasing concatenation parameter. In particular
the number of components equals the number of cycles of $\pi$.

**The standard axis and fixed framing.** In
$S^3=\{(z,w)\in\mathbb C^2:|z|^2+|w|^2=1\}$, as in
[[def-euclidean-spheres-and-closed-balls]], set
$$A=\{(0,w):|w|=1\},\qquad P_\theta=\{(z,w)\in S^3:z\ne0,\ \arg z=\theta\}.$$
Fix the following particular diffeomorphism, including its disk framing:
$$\varphi([(x,t)])=  \bigl(\sqrt{1-|x|^2}\,e^{2\pi it},x\bigr):  V\longrightarrow S^3\setminus A.$$
Its inverse has disk coordinate $x=w$ and circle coordinate
$[t]=[\arg z/(2\pi)]$. Every $P_\theta$ is consequently an open disk.
The **raw topological oriented closure** is
$$\widehat\beta_{\mathrm{top}}=\varphi(\operatorname{cl}(\beta)).$$
This explicit $\varphi$ is part of the construction; the definition
does not allow an arbitrary page-preserving change of framing.

**Page intersections and smooth representatives.** The whole closure
meets every page in exactly $n$ points. A component belonging to a
$\pi$-cycle of length $k$ meets each page in exactly $k$ points:
at any fractional height it uses exactly those $k$ distinct strands.
The page coordinate of its concatenation is $[t]$, for
$t\in\mathbb R/k\mathbb Z$, so its oriented degree is $+k$.
If all disk-coordinate strand maps are smooth and have all positive-order derivatives
zero at their endpoints, their cycle concatenations have matching jets
at every seam. The page coordinate has nonzero derivative, so the
result is a smooth embedding of disjoint oriented circles, in the
sense of [[def-smooth-embedding]]. For an endpoint-flat smooth braid, its literal $\varphi$-image is therefore a smooth oriented link and is denoted $\widehat\beta$.

**Closure in the smooth oriented-link category.** The raw image need not be smooth, even if individual strands are smooth but their endpoint jets fail to match at the cycle seams. For an arbitrary continuous braid, assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ ([[def-countable-choice]]) and choose a smooth representative $\beta_s$ by [[lem-every-geometric-braid-is-braid-isotopic-to-a-smooth-braid]]. Make it endpoint-flat by composing all disk-coordinate strands with a fixed smooth nondecreasing $\psi:I\to I$, equal to $0$ near $0$ and $1$ near $1$. Interpolation of height maps $(1-u)t+u\psi(t)$ is an endpoint-fixed braid isotopy, because every strand is evaluated at the same height. The smooth-category closure of $\beta$ is the oriented-link isotopy class of this chosen model's literal $\varphi$-image; when a subset is needed, use that chosen closed-braid representative. Independence of the representative is proved by [[lem-closure-depends-only-on-the-braid-isotopy-class]]. Page and cycle properties refer to the chosen constructed closed braid, with the same number of strands and endpoint permutation as $\beta$.

If $\beta$ already has smooth strands with matching cycle-seam jets, in particular if it is endpoint-flat, its literal raw image is a smooth link and is retained as $\widehat\beta$. The raw quotient, fixed $\varphi$, finite cycles, page counts and trivial closures remain choice-free. Finite elementary words have explicit smooth endpoint-flat models, so forming their literal closures also requires no choice assumption; $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ is used for the general continuous-representative convention and its independence theorem.

**The trivial closure.** For the constant braid its circles are
$\{(\sqrt{1-q_j^2}e^{2\pi it},q_j):[t]\in\mathbb R/\mathbb Z\}$.
They are latitudes of the sphere
$S=\{(z,w)\in S^3:\operatorname{Im}w=0\}$, with
$\operatorname{Re}w=q_j$. Each northern cap
$C_j=\{p\in S:\operatorname{Re}w(p)\ge q_j\}$ is a smooth disk:
stereographic coordinates on $S$ give radius
$\sqrt{(1-q_j)/(1+q_j)}$ for this cap. To make their spanning disks
disjoint, let $e$ be the unit vector in the $\operatorname{Im}w$
direction, set $\varepsilon=\pi/16$ and
$f_j(p)=\varepsilon(\operatorname{Re}w(p)-q_j)$ on $C_j$, and use
$$F_j(p)=\cos(f_j(p))p+\sin(f_j(p))e.$$
The boundary is fixed. The tubular parametrization
$(p,s)\mapsto\cos(s)p+\sin(s)e$ is injective for $|s|<\pi/2$,
and $0\le f_j<\pi/8$. On overlapping caps, if $q_i<q_j$ then
$f_i-f_j=\varepsilon(q_j-q_i)>0$, so their graphs are disjoint.
Thus these are pairwise disjoint smooth spanning disks. The trivial
$n$-braid closes to the oriented $n$-component unlink; for $n=1$
this is the unknot.

At $n=0$ all strand and cycle unions are empty, every page has zero intersections,
and the closure is the empty link. The basepoint list and disk constructions
above then have no entries.

By [F8], its closure is one component. Cut the standard four-crossing figure-eight diagram along its projection regions and four crossing arcs. Above and below the diagram this produces two ideal balls: each crossing arc has four face-side copies, and every face is a diagram region. Gluing upper and lower faces with the same region label restores the cut-open complement, because each cut face and crossing-arc side is identified with exactly its original mate; the only unfilled points are the deleted knot arcs, which are ideal vertices. Collapsing the two bigon faces gives two tetrahedra. Recording the vertex matches on their four faces gives exactly the four maps in the statement.

By [F2], at $z_1=z_2=z_3=w_1=w_2=w_3=\omega$ every edge parameter is $\omega$. The first edge class has product $\omega^6=1$, and the second has product $\omega^6=1$; each class contains six edge copies, so its total dihedral angle is $6(\pi/3)=2\pi$.

Applying the four vertex maps identifies all eight tetrahedron vertices into one ideal vertex and the twelve tetrahedron edges into the two six-edge classes in the statement. To check the link vertices explicitly, write $u|v$ for the truncation corner at ideal vertex $u$ on edge $uv$. The four corner classes are $\{0|1,0|2,3|2,3'|1',3'|2',0'|1'\}$, $\{1|0,1'|3',2|0,2'|3',1'|0',2|3\}$, $\{1|2,1'|2',0|3,0'|2',1|3,0'|3'\}$, and $\{2|1,2'|1',3|0,2'|0',3|1,3'|0'\}$; these are disjoint and contain all $24$ link corners. Hence the link is connected, closed and orientable, and therefore is a torus.

Assume countable choice, as required for the smooth normal-bundle structure in the tubular-neighbourhood interface. Let $K:S^1\to S^3$ be a smooth oriented knot and let $\nu(K)=TS^3|_K/TK$ be its quotient normal bundle. Equip $\nu(K)$ with a chosen smooth fibre norm $\|\cdot\|$. Let $\Phi:\Omega\to S^3$ be a tubular-neighbourhood map from an open neighbourhood $\Omega$ of the zero section in $\nu(K)$ that restricts to the inclusion of $K$. For $\epsilon>0$, define the closed disk subbundle
$$
D_\epsilon\nu(K):=\{v\in\nu(K):\|v\|\le\epsilon\}.
$$
Choose $\epsilon$ so that $D_\epsilon\nu(K)\subseteq\Omega$, and set $N(K)=\Phi(D_\epsilon\nu(K))$. The fibre norm, tubular map, and radius are part of the chosen tubular data. The **exterior** of this chosen tube is
$$
E_K:=S^3\setminus\operatorname{int}_{S^3}N(K).
$$
Retain its boundary $T_K:=\partial E_K=\partial N(K)$, orient $E_K$ by restriction of the fixed orientation of $S^3$, and orient $T_K$ as the boundary of $E_K$. The choice of tubular map and radius is part of the input to this definition.

Let $M$ be a compact smooth $3$-manifold. A properly embedded surface is **two-sided** if it has a product neighbourhood $F\times[-1,1]$ in $M$. A **compressing disk** for a two-sided surface $F$ is an embedded disk $D\subset M$ with $\operatorname{int}(D)\cap F=\varnothing$ and $\partial D$ an essential simple closed curve in $F$; $F$ is **incompressible** if it has no compressing disk. A **boundary-compressing disk** is an embedded disk $D$ with $\partial D=\alpha\cup\beta$, where $\alpha=D\cap F$ is an arc not cutting off a disk in $F$, $\beta=D\cap\partial M$, and $\operatorname{int}(D)$ misses $F\cup\partial M$; $F$ is **boundary-incompressible** if it has no such disk. A surface is **boundary-parallel** if it cobounds a product with a subsurface of $\partial M$, and it is **essential** if it is incompressible, boundary-incompressible, and not boundary-parallel. $M$ is **irreducible** if every embedded $2$-sphere in its interior bounds an embedded $3$-ball in $M$. An incompressible torus is boundary-parallel if it cobounds a product $T^2\times[0,1]$ with a component of $\partial M$; $M$ is **atoroidal** if every incompressible torus is boundary-parallel. A **Seifert fibration** is a decomposition into circles with local models given by fibered solid tori; in the model $(D^2\times S^1)/\langle(z,w)\mapsto(e^{2\pi i/q}z,e^{2\pi ip/q}w)\rangle$, where $\gcd(p,q)=1$, the core fiber has multiplicity $q$. Fibers of multiplicity $1$ are **regular** and those of multiplicity greater than $1$ are **exceptional**. A finite family of pairwise disjoint incompressible tori is a **JSJ system** if every component obtained by cutting $M$ along the family is atoroidal or Seifert-fibered. It is **inclusion-minimal** if no proper subfamily is a JSJ system. Atoroidal does not mean hyperbolic.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $E_K$ be the compact connected orientable exterior of a smooth knot in $S^3$, with one torus boundary component. If $E_K$ is irreducible, its boundary is incompressible, $E_K$ is atoroidal, and $E_K$ is not Seifert-fibered, then $\operatorname{int}(E_K)$ admits a complete finite-volume Riemannian metric of constant sectional curvature $-1$ with one torus cusp. No conclusion is asserted for a torus or satellite knot unless its exterior satisfies all four topological hypotheses.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Use the upper half-space model $\mathbb H^3=\{(z,y):z\in\mathbb C,y>0\}$ with metric $(|dz|^2+dy^2)/y^2$. Let $\Gamma\le\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ be discrete and torsion-free, and suppose that it contains a subgroup $A\cong\mathbb Z^2$. Then $A$ fixes a unique ideal point. After conjugating that point to infinity, its full stabilizer $P=\operatorname{Stab}_\Gamma(\infty)$ consists of translations by a lattice $\Lambda\le\mathbb C$ of rank two. It is the unique maximal abelian subgroup containing $A$.

For a sufficiently large $R$, the quotient of the closed horoball $\{y\ge R\}$ by $P$ embeds properly in $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$. Its boundary is a compact torus, its interior is a cusp, and its volume is $\operatorname{area}(\mathbb C/\Lambda)/(2R^2)$. If $M$ has exactly one topological end, the complement of the open cusp has compact closure.

No finite-volume thin decomposition, abstract peripheral recognition, or rigidity theorem is assumed or concluded here. The rank-two subgroup and the quotient presentation of $M$ are hypotheses.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Every nonempty connected oriented complete Riemannian three-manifold of constant sectional curvature $-1$ is isometric to $\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ for a discrete torsion-free subgroup $\Gamma\le\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$. The covering is a universal Riemannian covering and identifies $\Gamma$ with the fundamental group up to the usual basepoint conjugacies. Its completeness and quotient presentation are conclusions from the stated metric hypotheses. The orientation-preserving isometry group of the model is $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ with its usual Möbius boundary action.

Assume AC. Use the upper half-space model $\mathbb H^3=\{(z,y):z\in\mathbb C,y>0\}$ with metric $(|dz|^2+dy^2)/y^2$. Let $\Gamma\le\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ be discrete and torsion-free, and suppose that it contains a subgroup $A\cong\mathbb Z^2$. Then $A$ fixes a unique ideal point. After conjugating that point to infinity, its full stabilizer $P=\operatorname{Stab}_\Gamma(\infty)$ consists of translations by a lattice $\Lambda\le\mathbb C$ of rank two. It is the unique maximal abelian subgroup containing $A$.

For a sufficiently large $R$, the quotient of the closed horoball $\{y\ge R\}$ by $P$ embeds properly in $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$. Its boundary is a compact torus, its interior is a cusp, and its volume is $\operatorname{area}(\mathbb C/\Lambda)/(2R^2)$. If $M$ has exactly one topological end, the complement of the open cusp has compact closure.

No finite-volume thin decomposition, abstract peripheral recognition, or rigidity theorem is assumed or concluded here. The rank-two subgroup and the quotient presentation of $M$ are hypotheses.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(M,g)$ be a **nonempty**, connected,
boundaryless Riemannian manifold, and let $d=d_g$ be its Riemannian distance.
The following conditions are equivalent.

1. The metric space $(M,d)$ is complete.
2. The Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ is geodesically complete.
3. For every $p\in M$, the fibre exponential domain is all of the tangent
   space: $\mathcal E_p=T_pM$.
4. There is a point $p_0\in M$ for which $\mathcal E_{p_0}=T_{p_0}M$.
5. Every closed bounded subset of the metric space $(M,d)$ is compact.

Whenever these conditions hold, every $x,y\in M$ are joined by a minimizing
geodesic. More exactly, there is $v\in T_xM$ with
$$
\exp_x(v)=y,\qquad |v|_{g_x}=d(x,y),
$$
and $t\mapsto\exp_x(tv)$ on $[0,1]$ has length $d(x,y)$.

The nonemptiness hypothesis is essential for this formulation: on the empty
manifold conditions 1--3 and 5 are vacuous, whereas condition 4 is false.

Such a $D$ preserves either a unique ideal point or a pair of ideal points, unless trivial. If $H$ is trivial, finite index and torsion-freeness make $D$ trivial. Its centralizer from [F2] puts that normal core into either the translations fixing the parabolic point of $z$ or the diagonal group fixing its loxodromic pair. It is abelian and has that unique common fixed set. Normality makes $D$ preserve that set. A discrete torsion-free group preserving a pair is cyclic: an element interchanging the pair has order two, and the remaining diagonal group is cyclic by [F2]. A group preserving one point consists either of translations or is cyclic loxodromic. For the latter assertion, conjugate a loxodromic element fixing that point to a dilation fixing infinity and zero. Its commutator with any affine map fixing infinity is a translation. A nonzero such translation, conjugated by contracting powers of the dilation, tends to the identity, impossible in a discrete group. Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC. Every nonempty connected oriented complete Riemannian three-manifold of constant sectional curvature $-1$ is isometric to $\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ for a discrete torsion-free subgroup $\Gamma\le\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$. The covering is a universal Riemannian covering and identifies $\Gamma$ with the fundamental group up to the usual basepoint conjugacies. Its completeness and quotient presentation are conclusions from the stated metric hypotheses. The orientation-preserving isometry group of the model is $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ with its usual Möbius boundary action.

Assume AC. Let $M$ be a nonempty connected oriented complete Riemannian three-manifold of constant curvature $-1$ and finite volume. Then $M$ is a compact core together with finitely many pairwise disjoint standard torus cusp ends. Each end is an embedded quotient $\{y>R_i\}/\Lambda_i$ of a horoball by a rank-two translation lattice, and the complement of these open ends is compact. The number of cusps may be zero. In particular, the standard cusp decomposition in the general rigidity construction follows from the complete finite-volume metric, with no knot or triangulation assumption.

Assume AC. Let $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ and $N=\Gamma'\backslash\mathbb H^3$ be connected orientable hyperbolic manifolds, with discrete torsion-free groups. Suppose each is a compact core together with finitely many disjoint standard torus cusp ends: an end is an embedded quotient $\{y>R_i\}/\Lambda_i$ by a rank-two translation lattice, and the complement of the union of these ends is compact. Zero ends are allowed, in which case the manifold is compact.

Every group isomorphism $\theta:\Gamma\to\Gamma'$ permutes the conjugacy classes of the peripheral cusp groups. There is a smooth $\theta$-equivariant quasi-isometry $F:\mathbb H^3\to\mathbb H^3$ which on every sufficiently deep lifted cusp is affine in its horizontal coordinates and preserves cusp depth after a constant height rescaling. It has a smooth equivariant quasi-inverse with inverse affine cusp maps. On quotient manifolds these maps are proper homotopy equivalences.

The standard cusp decomposition is a supplied hypothesis here; this lemma does not derive it merely from finite volume.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. On $\mathbb H^3=\{(z,s):z\in\mathbb C,\ s>0\}$ use the metric $s^{-2}(|dz|^2+ds^2)$. Suppose $f:\mathbb H^3\to\mathbb H^3$ is a quasi-isometry with constants $\lambda\ge1$, $\varepsilon\ge0$:
$$\lambda^{-1}d(x,y)-\varepsilon\le d(f(x),f(y))\le\lambda d(x,y)+\varepsilon,$$
and with coarsely dense image. Then it induces an ideal-boundary homeomorphism $h:\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$. There is $H=H(\lambda,\varepsilon)<\infty$ such that, after postcomposition by any Möbius transformation carrying $h(\infty)$ to $\infty$, its plane restriction satisfies
$$\max_{|a-z|=r}|h(a)-h(z)|\le H\min_{|a-z|=r}|h(a)-h(z)|\qquad(z\in\mathbb C,\ r>0).$$
Here $h$ in that inequality denotes the normalized map. If the boundary homeomorphism preserves orientation, it is analytically quasiconformal in sphere charts, with constant at most $H$. If it reverses orientation, postcomposition with complex conjugation is quasiconformal with that constant. If $f$ is equivariant for a homomorphism between groups of hyperbolic isometries, its boundary map is equivariant for their boundary actions.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $G=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ act on the Riemann sphere by Möbius transformations. Let $\Gamma\le G$ be discrete, with finite nonzero Haar quotient measure $\nu$ on $X=\Gamma\backslash G$. Here Haar quotient measure means the right invariant Radon measure obtained by locally transporting Haar measure through the covering projection $G\to X$; its normalization is immaterial. Let $\theta:\Gamma\to G$ be a homomorphism, and let $h:\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$ be an orientation-preserving quasiconformal homeomorphism satisfying $h\circ\gamma=\theta(\gamma)\circ h$ for every $\gamma\in\Gamma$. Then $h$ is Möbius.

This statement assumes the existence of the quasiconformal boundary conjugacy. It does not assert that an abstract group isomorphism or a quasi-isometry produces one.

Assume countable choice. Let $M$ and $N$ be second-countable oriented hyperbolic three-manifolds, and let $f:M\to N$ be an isometry. Then
$$
\int_M d\operatorname{vol}_M=\int_N d\operatorname{vol}_N.
$$
In particular, if either volume is finite, then both are finite and the values agree.

derivations.claim: First use [F5] to write $M=\Gamma\backslash\mathbb H^3$ and $N=\Gamma'\backslash\mathbb H^3$ with the standard cusp decompositions, identifying their deck groups with the fundamental groups and transporting $\theta$ accordingly. We verify the finite-Haar hypothesis of [F3], rather than infer it from a citation. Put $G=\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ and $K=\mathrm{SO}(3)$, the stabilizer of a point in $\mathbb H^3$. The action identifies $G$ with the oriented orthonormal frame bundle: in the ball model an orientation-preserving isometry can send the center to any point by an upper half-space affine map after Cayley conjugation, and its stabilizer acts as every rotation; an isometry fixing a frame fixes each geodesic with its initial velocity and is the identity. Give $K$ normalized bi-invariant volume from the Ad-invariant inner product $-\operatorname{tr}(XY)$ on $\mathfrak{so}(3)$. Integrating this probability measure on each frame fiber against hyperbolic volume defines a smooth positive measure on $G$. It is independent of the local frame section, since changes of section are rotations, and is left-$G$-invariant, since $G$ acts isometrically on the base and by rotations on the fibers. It is also right invariant: in left-invariant tangent coordinates the Jacobian of right translation is $|\det_{\mathbb R}\operatorname{Ad}(g^{-1})|$. On $\mathfrak{sl}_2(\mathbb C)$ the complex determinant of Ad is one. For diagonal matrices its eigenvalues are $a^2,1,a^{-2}$; for upper and lower unipotent matrices Ad is triangular with diagonal entries one. These matrices generate $G$ by Gaussian elimination, so the determinant assertion holds for every $g$. The real determinant is the squared modulus of the complex one. Thus the displayed frame measure is Haar on both sides. Its quotient on $\Gamma\backslash G$ is the locally transported right invariant Radon measure required in [F3]. We give the uniqueness argument, including orientation reversal. First, $\Gamma$ is not elementary. A discrete torsion-free subgroup preserving a point at infinity consists either of translations or, if it contains a loxodromic element, is cyclic after conjugating that element to a diagonal form. In the latter case, the commutator of that loxodromic element with any affine map fixing infinity is a translation. If nontrivial it gives, by conjugation with contracting powers, nontrivial elements tending to the identity. Thus all elements also fix the loxodromic element’s second endpoint, and the diagonal subgroup is cyclic by the compact-annulus argument. The translation case has rank at most two, by the elementary lattice proof in [F1]'s supplier. A subgroup preserving just a pair of ideal points is also cyclic: an element interchanging them has order two in $\mathrm{PSL}_2(\mathbb C)$ and is excluded, and the remaining diagonal subgroup is cyclic by the compact-annulus argument in that same proof. All these quotients have infinite volume. For rank-two translations integrate $y^{-3}$ over a Euclidean fundamental parallelogram and $y\downarrow0$; rank-one translations have in addition an infinite horizontal direction. A cyclic loxodromic quotient has cylindrical density $\sinh r\cosh r\,dr\,d\varphi\,dt$ about its axis, with $t$ taken modulo its positive translation length, so integrating over $r\to\infty$ diverges even if its generator rotates the cylinder. The trivial quotient is $\mathbb H^3$ and has infinite volume as well. These direct integrations contradict the given finite volume.

Apply [F1] to $\theta$, then [F2] to its equivariant quasi-isometry, to get an equivariant boundary homeomorphism $h$. If $h$ preserves orientation, [F3] and step 1.1 make it Möbius. The boundary map $Rh$ is orientation preserving and quasiconformal; its target representation is $\gamma\mapsto R\theta(\gamma)R^{-1}$ in $G$. Apply [F3] to get that $Rh$ is Möbius. If an orientation-preserving isometry $J$ centralizes $\Gamma$ and is nonidentity, its Möbius action is parabolic or has two distinct eigenlines. In the parabolic case its centralizer consists of translations fixing its ideal point. Such an interchange has order two, so does not belong to the torsion-free $\Gamma$. Consequently centralizing $J$ would make $\Gamma$ elementary, contrary to step 1.2. Two isometries inducing the same outer isomorphism have lifts whose induced isomorphisms agree after a target deck transformation. Their quotient then centralizes $\Gamma$, so they are equal.

The descended $F$ and $I$ are properly homotopic. Unique geodesics give an equivariant homotopy with bounded tracks. > Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(M,g)$ be a **nonempty**, connected,
boundaryless Riemannian manifold, and let $d=d_g$ be its Riemannian distance.
The following conditions are equivalent.

1. The metric space $(M,d)$ is complete.
2. The Riemannian manifold $(M,g)$ is geodesically complete.
3. For every $p\in M$, the fibre exponential domain is all of the tangent
   space: $\mathcal E_p=T_pM$.
4. There is a point $p_0\in M$ for which $\mathcal E_{p_0}=T_{p_0}M$.
5. Every closed bounded subset of the metric space $(M,d)$ is compact.

Whenever these conditions hold, every $x,y\in M$ are joined by a minimizing
geodesic. More exactly, there is $v\in T_xM$ with
$$
\exp_x(v)=y,\qquad |v|_{g_x}=d(x,y),
$$
and $t\mapsto\exp_x(tv)$ on $[0,1]$ has length $d(x,y)$.

The nonemptiness hypothesis is essential for this formulation: on the empty
manifold conditions 1--3 and 5 are vacuous, whereas condition 4 is false.

Hence the injectivity radii of their images in $M$ tend to zero. On every compact subset of $M$ the injectivity radius is bounded below by a positive constant: each point has an evenly covered small metric ball, and finitely many smaller such balls cover a compact set. Thus this escaping sequence cannot have its image in a compact set. Sequential compactness in metric spaces proves properness. The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume the inherited Axiom of Countable Choice $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let
$(M,g)$ be a connected, boundaryless, finite-dimensional Riemannian manifold
that is complete and whose sectional curvature satisfies $K\le0$ at every
tangent two-plane. Then for every $p\in M$:

1. the exponential map $\exp_p:T_pM\to M$ is a smooth covering map when its
   domain carries the pulled-back metric $\tilde g:=\exp_p^*g$;
2. $(T_pM,\tilde g)$ is complete and $T_pM$ is simply connected, so $\exp_p$ is
   a **universal cover** of $M$;
3. if in addition $M$ is simply connected, then $\exp_p$ is a diffeomorphism
   for every $p$, and $M$ is diffeomorphic to the Euclidean space $T_pM$.

The curvature sign is the one of [[def-sectional-curvature]], so $K\le0$
includes the flat case; no lower bound on curvature, no compactness and no
dimension restriction (other than finiteness) are assumed. The completeness of
$(T_pM,\tilde g)$ is a conclusion, not a hypothesis: without it the pulled-back
metric need not be complete even for a local diffeomorphism of a complete
manifold.

Assume exactly $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$. Let $(M,g)$ be a smooth Riemannian
manifold without boundary, let $p\in M$, let $v\in\mathcal E_p$ be in the
domain of $\exp_p$, and let $w\in T_pM$. Define
$$\gamma:[0,1]\to M,\qquad \gamma(t)=\exp_p(tv).$$
There is a unique Jacobi field $J$ along $\gamma$ with
$$J(0)=0,\qquad D_tJ(0)=w,$$
where the derivative at $0$ is one-sided. For every $t\in[0,1]$,
$$J(t)=d(\exp_p)_{tv}(tw),$$
using the canonical identification $T_{tv}(\mathcal E_p)\cong T_pM$,
and in particular $d(\exp_p)_v(w)=J(1)$. The exponential differential is
evaluated at points $tv\in\mathcal E_p$, as ensured by the geodesic-time
scaling property. Constant central geodesics, zero initial data, and dimension
zero are included. No completeness hypothesis is imposed.

This item assumes $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, namely [[def-countable-choice|countable choice]]. In the propagated dependency chain, that assumption is required through [[def-constant-sectional-curvature-and-space-form]]; the tensor-determination argument is choice-free.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ as inherited through
[[def-constant-sectional-curvature-and-space-form]]; the algebraic proof below
uses no additional choice. A Riemannian manifold has constant sectional
curvature $K$ if and only if

$$R(X,Y)Z=K\bigl(g(Y,Z)X-g(X,Z)Y\bigr).$$

Equivalently,

$$\operatorname{Rm}(X,Y,Z,W)=K\bigl(g(Y,Z)g(X,W)-g(X,Z)g(Y,W)\bigr).$$

Let $\gamma:I\to M$ be smooth on an interval, with smooth one-sided data at included endpoints. For every $t_0\in I$ and $v_0\in E_{\gamma(t_0)}$ there is exactly one parallel section $V$ on all of $I$ with $V(t_0)=v_0$. The same holds for a piecewise smooth curve on a compact interval, with continuity at its finitely many corners. A singleton carries its prescribed vector. No AC is required for a supplied connection and curve.

Let $(M,g)$ be an $n$-dimensional Riemannian manifold, let $I\subseteq\mathbb R$
be an interval with nonempty interior, and let $\gamma:I\to M$ be an
affinely parametrized geodesic. For every $a\in I$ and every
$v,w\in T_{\gamma(a)}M$, there is exactly one smooth Jacobi field $J$ along
all of $\gamma$ such that
$$J(a)=v,\qquad D_tJ(a)=w.$$
If $a$ is an included endpoint, $D_tJ(a)$ is interpreted one-sided. Constant
geodesics and dimension zero are included. The result requires no completeness,
compactness of $I$, or axiom of choice.

Levi–Civita parallel transport preserves inner products, lengths, angles of nonzero vectors, and Riemannian volume density. If the manifold is oriented, it also preserves its oriented Riemannian volume form. Without a supplied global orientation only density preservation is claimed.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. On $\mathbb H^3=\{(z,s):z\in\mathbb C,\ s>0\}$ use the metric $s^{-2}(|dz|^2+ds^2)$. Suppose $f:\mathbb H^3\to\mathbb H^3$ is a quasi-isometry with constants $\lambda\ge1$, $\varepsilon\ge0$:
$$\lambda^{-1}d(x,y)-\varepsilon\le d(f(x),f(y))\le\lambda d(x,y)+\varepsilon,$$
and with coarsely dense image. Then it induces an ideal-boundary homeomorphism $h:\widehat{\mathbb C}\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$. There is $H=H(\lambda,\varepsilon)<\infty$ such that, after postcomposition by any Möbius transformation carrying $h(\infty)$ to $\infty$, its plane restriction satisfies
$$\max_{|a-z|=r}|h(a)-h(z)|\le H\min_{|a-z|=r}|h(a)-h(z)|\qquad(z\in\mathbb C,\ r>0).$$
Here $h$ in that inequality denotes the normalized map. If the boundary homeomorphism preserves orientation, it is analytically quasiconformal in sphere charts, with constant at most $H$. If it reverses orientation, postcomposition with complex conjugation is quasiconformal with that constant. If $f$ is equivariant for a homomorphism between groups of hyperbolic isometries, its boundary map is equivariant for their boundary actions.

Proof, step 3.1: By [F2] and step 2.1, $f$ induces a homeomorphism of sequence boundaries. In this model that boundary is the ordinary ideal sphere. For precision, in the ball every geodesic ray from the origin is radial by step 1.1 and is parameterized as $u(r)=\tanh(r/2)\omega$, $|\omega|=1$. Substitution in the distance formula gives the product limit $(\omega|\omega')_0=-\log(|\omega-\omega'|/2)$ for distinct unit vectors and infinity for equal ones. Thus its product topology is the ordinary sphere topology, and finite-distance asymptotic rays have the same endpoint. By properness and [F2], every sequence-boundary class has a ray representative, and the uniform-on-bounded-interval topology of the radial rays is the ordinary topology of their unit endpoints. Consequently [F2]'s extension is exactly the ideal-boundary homeomorphism, and $x_n\to a$ ideally implies $f(x_n)\to h(a)$ whenever $(x_n)$ runs to infinity along a geodesic ray. [A1, F2, step 1.1, step 2.1, algebra]

An isometry with identity boundary action fixes intersections of complete geodesics and is the identity. Proof, step 1.1: We first give the model geometry used below. Translations, complex rotations and positive dilations act by $(z,s)\mapsto(az+b,|a|s)$ and preserve the metric by substitution. Euclidean inversion in the unit sphere, followed by reflection in a vertical plane, is $(z,s)\mapsto(-\overline z/(|z|^2+s^2),s/(|z|^2+s^2))$ and extends $z\mapsto-1/z$. Its Euclidean differential scales lengths by $(|z|^2+s^2)^{-1}$, while its height scales by the same factor, so it also preserves the hyperbolic metric. These maps generate all Möbius transformations: a matrix with nonzero lower-left entry gives a translation, an inversion, a complex dilation and a translation by elementary fraction division; a zero lower-left entry gives an affine map. Thus every boundary Möbius transformation extends to an isometry. The Cayley map $T(z,s)=(2\operatorname{Re}z,2\operatorname{Im}z,|z|^2+s^2-1)/(|z|^2+(s+1)^2)$ is a bijection onto the unit ball, with inverse $z=2(u_1+iu_2)/Q$, $s=(1-|u|^2)/Q$, $Q=u_1^2+u_2^2+(1-u_3)^2$. It carries $(0,1)$ to the origin and gives metric $4|du|^2/(1-|u|^2)^2$: its Euclidean length factor is $2/(|z|^2+(s+1)^2)$ and $1-|T|^2=4s/(|z|^2+(s+1)^2)$. Radial integration in the ball, together with $|(|u|)'|\le|u'|$ on every competing path, gives distance $2\operatorname{artanh}|u|$ from the origin. Applying the affine normalization of a general basepoint yields $\cosh d((z,s),(w,t))=\frac{|z-w|^2+s^2+t^2}{2st}.$ Equality in that radial length argument characterizes the radial segment. Its inverse Cayley image shows that geodesics are the vertical lines and the Euclidean semicircles orthogonal to the boundary. In particular geodesics are unique, closed bounded hyperbolic balls are compact by the displayed formula, and the ideal endpoints of a complete geodesic are its distinct Euclidean boundary endpoints. A complete geodesic is uniquely determined by those endpoints. Consequently an isometry with identity boundary action preserves every complete geodesic and fixes the intersection of two distinct complete geodesics through each point; it is the identity. Thus the Möbius extension constructed above is unique. [given, algebra]

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

Assume AC for the projection-family proof below. For $\lambda\ge1$, $\varepsilon\ge0$ and $\delta\ge0$, the image of every possibly discontinuous $(\lambda,\varepsilon)$-quasi-geodesic map of a nonempty compact real interval into a geodesic $\delta$-slim space has Hausdorff distance at most
$$M=92\lambda^2(\varepsilon+3\delta)$$
from every geodesic with the same endpoints. No properness is assumed.

Assume AC for the Morse/coarse-inverse proof. A quasi-isometry between geodesic hyperbolic spaces induces a homeomorphism of their Gromov-sequence boundaries; bounded-distance maps induce the same map and extensions respect composition. Properness is needed for the compact ray-boundary package, not imposed on this sequence statement.

Assume AC. Let $X$ be a nonempty proper geodesic space with a product hyperbolicity constant $\kappa\ge0$, and fix $o\in X$. Proper means every closed ball of positive finite radius is compact. Every Gromov-sequence class has a geodesic ray representative $r:[0,\infty)\to X$ with $r(0)=o$, represented by $(r(n))_{n\ge1}$. The quotient of these rays by finite Hausdorff distance, with the topology induced from uniform convergence on bounded parameter intervals, is homeomorphic to the Gromov-sequence boundary with its product topology. In particular the boundary is compact, including when it is empty.

In coordinates for a Riemannian metric with matrix $(g_{ij})$ and inverse $(g^{ij})$, its Levi–Civita symbols are
$$\Gamma^k{}_{ij}=\tfrac12\sum_\ell g^{k\ell}(\partial_i g_{j\ell}+\partial_j g_{i\ell}-\partial_\ell g_{ij}).$$

Assume the axiom of choice. Let $(M,g,J)$ be an oriented Riemannian surface and let $T\subseteq M$ be a
compact regular oriented disk region with exactly three vertices whose boundary
is the cyclic concatenation of three regular $C^2$ embedded geodesic segments
of the interior metric; at each vertex the incoming and outgoing one-sided unit
tangents are not antipodal. Suppose that a neighbourhood of $T$ carries a
smooth positive orthonormal frame and that $T$ is positively oriented as a disk
region. If $\alpha,\beta,\gamma\in(0,2\pi)$ are the interior sector angles at
the three vertices, then

$$\int_TK\,dA=\alpha+\beta+\gamma-\pi .$$

The boundary orientation is the outward-normal-first orientation of
[[def-regular-oriented-surface-region-with-piecewise-smooth-boundary]], and no
claim is made about the existence of such a triangle on a general surface.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $h:\mathbb C\to\mathbb C$ be an orientation-preserving homeomorphism. For $x\in\mathbb C$ and $r>0$, put $L(x,r)=\max_{|y-x|=r}|h(y)-h(x)|$ and $l(x,r)=\min_{|y-x|=r}|h(y)-h(x)|$. Suppose $L(x,r)\le H l(x,r)$ for every $x,r$, with one fixed $1\le H<\infty$. Then $h\in W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}$, its continuous representative is ACL, and it is analytically $H$-quasiconformal:
$$|h_{\bar z}|\le\frac{H-1}{H+1}|h_z|\quad\hbox{almost everywhere}.$$
For relatively compact open sets $V\Subset U\Subset\mathbb C$, a coordinate unit vector $e_i$ and $0<|t|<\operatorname{dist}(V,\partial U)/2$, one has the explicit estimate
$$\int_V\left|\frac{h(x+te_i)-h(x)}t\right|^2\,dx\le4H^2\operatorname{area}(h(U)).$$

boundaries.evidence: Finite positive quotient measure is assumed, so the bounded Beltrami lift is a genuineL2 vector. Proof, step 2.2: Outside the Haar-null set where $g(0)=\infty$, define $F(g)=\mu(g(0))\overline{g'(0)}/g'(0)$, and put it equal to zero on that exceptional set. This is bounded and measurable. Step 1.2 and the holomorphic chain rule give $F(\gamma g)=F(g)$ for almost every $g$, for each $\gamma$. Because $\Gamma$ is countable, remove the union of the exceptional sets and all their $\Gamma$ translates; this is an invariant Haar-null set. Redefining $F$ as zero on it gives an exactly left-$\Gamma$-invariant representative. It descends to a measurable bounded function on $X$: on each quotient chart use a local section of the covering projection, and exact invariance makes the resulting definitions agree. Finite measure gives $F\in L^2(X,\nu)$. [A1, step 1.1, step 1.2, algebra]

Rotation bypi/2 forces the constant lifted Beltrami coefficient equal to its negative and hence zero. Proof, step 6.1: In the finite source coordinate, $a_t(z)=e^tz$, so $a_t$ fixes $0$ and has positive real derivative there. Consequently $F(ga_t)=F(g)$ for Haar-almost every $g$, for every $t$; the redefinition in step 2.2 changes this only on a null set and its right translate. Thus $R_{a_t}F=F$ in $L^2(X)$, and steps 3.1–5.1 imply $F=c$ almost everywhere for a complex constant $c$. Now let $m_\theta(z)=e^{i\theta}z$. The same computation gives $F(gm_\theta)=e^{-2i\theta}F(g)$ almost everywhere. Right translation preserves the measure class, so the constant satisfies $c=e^{-2i\theta}c$ for every $\theta$. Taking $\theta=\pi/2$ gives $c=-c$, hence $c=0$. [step 3.1, step 4.1, step 5.1, step 2.2, algebra]

The resulting1-quasiconformal map is holomorphic and therefore Mobius on the sphere. Proof, step 7.1: Since the derivative ratio in step 2.2 has modulus one, $F=0$ Haar-almost everywhere implies $\mu\circ p=0$ Haar-almost everywhere. The positive-area converse in step 1.2 forces $\mu=0$ area-almost everywhere. By [F4], $h$ is holomorphic in every finite source and target chart. The finitely many omitted chart points cause no issue: use alternate source and target charts there and the conformal coefficient transformation law [F3]; their exceptional sets remain null. Thus $h$ is a biholomorphic sphere homeomorphism and is Möbius by [F4]. [F3, F4, step 1.2, step 2.2, step 6.1, algebra] ∎

Sphere chart singularities and pullbacks of area-null exceptional sets are treated through submersion coordinates and Fubini. Proof, step 1.2: Let $\mu$ be the Beltrami coefficient of $h$ in the standard finite source coordinate, defined arbitrarily on its null exceptional set, with $|\mu|\le k<1$. Finite source and target charts suffice outside at most finitely many points. Since holomorphic coordinate changes obey [F3], the conjugacy identity gives $\mu(\gamma z)\overline{\gamma'(z)}/\gamma'(z)=\mu(z)$ almost everywhere, for every $\gamma\in\Gamma$. Consider the evaluation map $p:G\to\widehat{\mathbb C}$, $p(g)=g(0)$. It is a smooth submersion: infinitesimal translations span the tangent plane at $0$, and left translation transports that statement to every $g$. Its local coordinates are a product of a sphere chart and a four-dimensional fiber chart; Haar measure has a smooth positive density in these coordinates. Thus inverse images under $p$ of area-null sets are Haar null by Fubini; conversely a positive-area set has inverse image of positive Haar measure in some such product chart. [A1, F2, F3, given, algebra]

derivations.claim: The quotient $X$ is a second-countable smooth manifold: left translation by a discrete subgroup is free, and each point of $G$ has a small open neighborhood disjoint from its nontrivial left translates. The projection restricts to a diffeomorphism there, giving the quotient charts. A Borel set in $X$ is $\nu$-null exactly when its full inverse image is Haar null, by the local quotient definition of $\nu$, countable quotient charts and countability of $\Gamma$. $$ \partial_z f:=\frac12(\partial_x f-i\partial_y f)=\frac12(u_x+v_y)+\frac{i}{2}(v_x-u_y), $$

$$ \partial_{\bar z}f:=\frac12(\partial_x f+i\partial_y f)=\frac12(u_x-v_y)+\frac{i}{2}(v_x+u_y). $$

Real total differentiability means total differentiability of $\widetilde f$ under [[def-total-derivative-in-euclidean-space]], with a real-linear derivative as in [[def-euclidean-linear-map]]. Its transported real-linear map $Df$ is supplied by [[thm-complex-coordinate-map-preserves-real-total-differentiability]]. If $f$ is real totally differentiable, put $A=\partial_x f$ and $B=\partial_y f$. The remainder definition along the two coordinate axes gives $Df(1)=A$ and $Df(i)=B$. Real linearity then gives $Df(s+it)=sA+tB$ for real $s,t$, whereas direct expansion of $\frac12(A-iB)(s+it)+\frac12(A+iB)(s-it)$ gives the same expression. Thus

$$ Df(h)=(\partial_z f)h+(\partial_{\bar z}f)\overline h. $$

A real-differentiable map is **antiholomorphic** on $U$ when $\partial_z f=0$ at every point of $U$. Thus its differential is conjugate-linear at every point; no complex differentiability is asserted unless the other Wirtinger derivative also vanishes.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). Let $\Omega,\Omega'\subseteq\mathbb C$ be complex domains ([[def-complex-domain]]) and $f:\Omega\to\Omega'$ a homeomorphism ([[def-homeomorphism-and-open-maps]]). Read $f$ as a map into $\mathbb R^2$; continuity makes its components locally square integrable. Recall that $W^{1,2}_{\rm loc}(\Omega)$ ([[def-sobolev-space-wkp-and-its-norm]]) means that the components of $f$ admit weak first partial derivatives ([[def-weak-derivative-of-a-locally-integrable-function]]) in $L^2_{\rm loc}$; equivalently, their almost-everywhere classes have ACL representatives in both coordinate directions whose measurable classical coordinate derivatives belong to $L^2_{\rm loc}$ ([[def-absolute-continuity-on-almost-every-coordinate-line]], [[thm-acl-characterisation-of-w-one-p]]). ACL alone does not assert this derivative integrability. Countable Choice ([[def-countable-choice]]) is included in AC for the completed-product Fubini interfaces. On almost every coordinate line the continuous map $f$ agrees almost everywhere with its ACL representative, hence everywhere by continuity of both restrictions; its classical line derivatives then represent its weak derivatives.

Let $K\ge1$ and put $k=(K-1)/(K+1)\in[0,1)$. The homeomorphism $f$ is **$K$-quasiconformal in the analytic sense** when

(A1) $f\in W^{1,2}_{\rm loc}(\Omega)$; and

(A2) its weak Wirtinger derivatives $\partial_zf,\partial_{\bar z}f$ ([[def-wirtinger-derivatives]]) lie in $L^2_{\rm loc}(\Omega)$ and satisfy
$$|\partial_{\bar z}f(z)|\le k|\partial_zf(z)|\qquad\text{for almost every }z\in\Omega.$$

The inequality is a statement about $L^2_{\rm loc}$ classes: it is independent of the choice of representative of $f$ and of the Borel representatives of its weak Wirtinger derivatives, since each such representative agrees almost everywhere with its class ([[lem-weak-derivative-is-independent-of-lp-representatives]]). The map is **analytically quasiconformal** if it is $K$-analytically quasiconformal for some finite $K$. Its minimal constant is recovered from the Beltrami coefficient defined later on this page.

**Orientation and the regularity requirement.** Inequality (A2) gives $J_f=|\partial_zf|^2-|\partial_{\bar z}f|^2\ge(1-k^2)|\partial_zf|^2\ge0$ almost everywhere, with respect to planar Lebesgue measure ([[def-nonnegative-lebesgue-integral]]). A classical derivative inequality alone does not replace (A1): on $(0,1)^2$, the map $f(x+iy)=x+g(x)+iy$, where $g$ is the Cantor function, is a homeomorphism onto $(0,2)\times(0,1)$ ([[lem-x-plus-the-cantor-function-is-a-homeomorphism-from-zero-one-onto-zero-two]]). The Cantor function is continuous, nonconstant, and locally constant off the null Cantor set, so $g'=0$ almost everywhere ([[thm-cantor-function-properties]], [[cor-cantor-set-is-an-uncountable-lebesgue-null-set]]). Thus the classical Wirtinger derivatives are $\partial_zf=1$ and $\partial_{\bar z}f=0$ almost everywhere. But $g$ cannot be absolutely continuous on every compact subinterval of $(0,1)$: the fundamental theorem would make it constant there, and then continuity would contradict $g(0)=0$, $g(1)=1$ ([[thm-fundamental-theorem-of-calculus-for-absolutely-continuous-functions]]). Subtracting the identity shows that $f$ fails ACL on every horizontal line and therefore fails (A1). Its classical inequality is not the weak-derivative assertion (A2). Orientation preservation follows from (A1) together with (A2), as proved by the equivalence theorem on this page.

derivations.claim: Define the locally finite Borel measure $\omega(E)=\operatorname{area}(h(E))$. This is a measure because a homeomorphism maps disjoint Borel sets to disjoint Borel sets and respects unions. It is Radon because it is the pushforward of planar area by the homeomorphism $h^{-1}$; compact and open approximation transport through that homeomorphism. The open image $h(B(x,r))$ contains $B(h(x),l(x,r))$: otherwise a segment from $h(x)$ to a point of that smaller disk outside the image would first meet the boundary $h(\partial B(x,r))$, contradicting the definition of $l$. The maximum distance from $h(x)$ in $h(\overline{B(x,r)})$ occurs on its boundary, because distance from a fixed point has no maximum in a nonempty open set. Hence $|h(y)-h(x)|\le L(x,r)\le H l(x,r)$ for $y\in\overline{B(x,r)}$, and $\pi l(x,r)^2\le\omega(B(x,r))$.

For $x\in V$ and $0<|t|<\operatorname{dist}(V,\partial U)/2$, use step 1.1 with radius $2|t|$ to obtain $|h(x+te_i)-h(x)|^2\le(H^2/\pi)\omega(B(x,2|t|))$. These balls lie in $U$. Tonelli, applied to their incidence indicator, gives $\int_V\omega(B(x,2|t|))\,dx=\int_U|V\cap B(y,2|t|)|\,d\omega(y)\le4\pi t^2\omega(U)$. Combining the two inequalities proves the explicit difference-quotient estimate. All measures in this calculation are locally finite Radon measures and the incidence set is open, so no absolute continuity or null-set preservation of $h$ has been presumed.

Continuity makes $h$ square integrable on every relatively compact $U$. The uniform estimate in step 2.1 and [F1], with $p=2$ and complex-valued functions, give $h\in W^{1,2}(V)$. Exhausting the plane proves local Sobolev regularity. Apply [F2] on a countable collection of rectangles. On almost every coordinate line, its ACL representative agrees with the continuous representative almost everywhere by Fubini, hence everywhere on each compact line interval because both are continuous there. Thus the actual map $h$ is ACL and has finite coordinate partial derivatives almost everywhere, agreeing with the weak derivatives.

By the general-homeomorphism interface [F3], $h$ is totally differentiable almost everywhere. At such a point $x$, write $h(x+v)=h(x)+Av+o(|v|)$; the remainder is uniform over $|v|=r$ after division by $r$. If $A$ has rank one, there are unit vectors $u,v$ with $Au=0$ and $|Av|>0$. Then $l(x,r)=o(r)$ whereas $L(x,r)\ge r|Av|+o(r)$, contradicting the finite circular bound. If $A$ is nonsingular with singular values $s_1\ge s_2>0$, the same uniform expansion gives $L(x,r)/r\to s_1$ and $l(x,r)/r\to s_2$, so $s_1/s_2\le H$. Its determinant is positive by [F3], since $h$ preserves orientation. The remaining possibility is $A=0$.

At almost every point the classical partials of the total derivative equal the weak derivatives by step 3.1. At the nonsingular points, [F5] and step 4.1 give $|h_{\bar z}|/|h_z|\le(H-1)/(H+1)$; at zero derivatives the asserted inequality also holds. Together with $W^{1,2}_{\mathrm{loc}}$ and ACL regularity, this is exactly analytic $H$-quasiconformality. The proof uses only the locally proved total-differentiability interface [F3]; it does not invoke an infinitesimal metric-to-quasiconformal criterion.
